metadata.name: ATLAS English Academy
metadata.description: Original instructional mini-lessons, reading passages, and graded exercises for 16 learning levels.
metadata.scoreNote: Objective items automatically scored. Short responses and writing receive provisional, explainable keyword/structure estimates, not semantic judgment.

strands.name: Sound, Print & Language Systems
strands.description: Hear and recognize sounds, words, spelling patterns, and the systems of language.

strands.name: Decoding, Fluency & Spelling
strands.description: Read accurately, decode unfamiliar words, and develop fluent phrasing.

strands.name: Vocabulary & Word Formation
strands.description: Understand precise meanings, context clues, roots, registers, and word choice.

strands.name: Grammar, Syntax & Style
strands.description: Build effective sentences and edit conventions from basic to advanced syntax.

strands.name: Fiction & Literary Analysis
strands.description: Interpret characters, conflicts, structure, themes, narrators, and literary choices.

strands.name: Poetry, Drama & Figurative Language
strands.description: Recognize sound, rhythm, imagery, metaphor, voice, and performance.

strands.name: Informational & Technical Reading
strands.description: Analyze explanatory and technical texts, diagrams, purposes, and structures.

strands.name: Close Reading & Textual Evidence
strands.description: Make inferences, distinguish evidence and claims, and support interpretations.

strands.name: Writing Process & Revision
strands.description: Plan, draft, organize, edit, revise, and reflect on effective prose.

strands.name: Argumentation & Rhetoric
strands.description: State claims, provide reasons and evidence, address alternatives, and analyze persuasion.

strands.name: Research, Media & Citation
strands.description: Ask questions, locate reliable sources, synthesize findings, and credit others.

strands.name: Speaking, Listening & Communication
strands.description: Listen actively, speak clearly, discuss ideas, and adapt to an audience.

lessons.passage: Mia was at the school playground. Mia said the sounds at the start of sun and sand. Both words began with the same /s/ sound. Mia found two matching sounds.

glossary.definition: words with matching ending sounds

noticed fresh muddy footprints near a watering can

sounded out map and tap one sound at a time

questions.explanation: Return to the sentence describing what the person actually did. Evidence must come from the text.

questions.prompt: What did the person notice?

the sounds joined to make whole words
the owner smiled and thanked Nia

questions.explanation: The observation is a reported detail; it is not the broadest possible conclusion.

lessons.title: Explain how syllable patterns guide pronunciation
lessons.objective: Learners will explain how syllable patterns guide pronunciation.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to explain how syllable patterns guide pronunciation. A spoken word is made of sounds; print represents language with letters and combinations of letters. A phoneme is a contrastive speech sound. A grapheme is a written symbol or symbol group. English spelling is patterned, but spelling and sound are not identical. Worked example: Say “ship” slowly: /sh/ /i/ /p/. The letters s and h jointly represent the first sound. Pronunciation differences among dialects are systematic, not evidence of poor intelligence. Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to revise clarity, sequence, and sensory detail. Writing improves through planning, drafting, reading for a reader’s needs, and focused revision. lessons.title: Explain how evidence supports an interpretation
lessons.objective: Learners will explain how evidence supports an interpretation.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to explain how evidence supports an interpretation. An inference is a conclusion supported by observations, not a guess presented as fact. Evidence must be accurate, relevant, and explained. Quotations and paraphrases should preserve the author’s meaning. Worked example: “The lamp was still warm” may support a recent-use inference, but does not alone establish who used it. Cite the observation, explain the reasoning, and name uncertainty. Strategy: Claim → cited detail → reasoning → limitation or competing explanation.

lessons.title: Distinguish phonemes, graphemes, and allophones
lessons.objective: Learners will distinguish phonemes, graphemes, and allophones.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to distinguish phonemes, graphemes, and allophones. A spoken word is made of sounds; print represents language with letters and combinations of letters. A phoneme is a contrastive speech sound. A grapheme is a written symbol or symbol group. English spelling is patterned, but spelling and sound are not identical. Worked example: Say “ship” slowly: /sh/ /i/ /p/. The letters s and h jointly represent the first sound. Pronunciation differences among dialects are systematic, not evidence of poor intelligence. Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

lessons.passage: In the middle school language club, Ari recorded different pronunciations of the same word. Students pronounced some vowels differently but understood one another. The explanation matters: pronunciation varies across communities and contexts. The club described systematic differences without ranking speakers. The passage advances a central principle: language variation is patterned and should not be treated as a defect. Yet the evidence has a boundary: a small club cannot represent every dialect. Consequently, the group planned to sample speakers from more communities. The reader should distinguish the reported observation from the interpretation offered to explain it.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to improve phrasing, accuracy, and reading rate. Fluency also requires accuracy, phrasing, and expression; reading quickly without comprehension is not the goal. Worked example: In “unhelpful,” identify un- + help + -ful. Strategy: Mark unfamiliar word parts, blend, reread the whole sentence, and summarize what it means.

lessons.title: Distinguish claim, evidence, and reasoning
lessons.objective: Learners will distinguish claim, evidence, and reasoning.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to distinguish claim, evidence, and reasoning. An argument is a justified claim, not merely a strong opinion. Distinguish claims, evidence, warrants, counterarguments, and rhetorical appeals. Good reasoning explains why evidence supports the conclusion. Worked example: Claim: “The park should add shade.” Evidence: “Visitors reported heat exposure.” Warrant: “Shade lowers direct sun exposure.” A complete argument acknowledges costs and alternatives. Strategy: State a claim, give specific evidence, explain its relevance, and address a fair objection.

lessons.title: Explain dialect variation without judging speakers
lessons.objective: Learners will explain dialect variation without judging speakers.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to explain dialect variation without judging speakers. A spoken word is made of sounds; print represents language with letters and combinations of letters. A phoneme is a contrastive speech sound. A grapheme is a written symbol or symbol group. English spelling is patterned, but spelling and sound are not identical. Worked example: Say “ship” slowly: /sh/ /i/ /p/. The letters s and h jointly represent the first sound. Pronunciation differences among dialects are systematic, not evidence of poor intelligence. Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

Worked example: Instead of “That is wrong,” try “I heard your claim that the garden needs more water. What measurement supports it?” The second response tests evidence without attacking the person. Strategy: Prepare an opening, supporting points, and a conclusion; listen; confirm understanding.

lessons.title: Analyze spelling changes across English history
lessons.objective: Learners will analyze spelling changes across English history.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to analyze spelling changes across English history. A spoken word is made of sounds; print represents language with letters and combinations of letters. A phoneme is a contrastive speech sound. A grapheme is a written symbol or symbol group. English spelling is patterned, but spelling and sound are not identical. Worked example: Say “ship” slowly: /sh/ /i/ /p/. The letters s and h jointly represent the first sound. Pronunciation differences among dialects are systematic, not evidence of poor intelligence. Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to explain how morphology supports efficient decoding. Decode by connecting spelling patterns to sounds, blending, and checking the resulting word against context. Fluency also requires accuracy, phrasing, and expression; reading quickly without comprehension is not the goal. Worked example: In “unhelpful,” identify un- + help + -ful. Strategy: Mark unfamiliar word parts, blend, reread the whole sentence, and summarize what it means.

Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

lessons.title: Analyze how form shapes argument and emotion
lessons.objective: Learners will analyze how form shapes argument and emotion.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to analyze how form shapes argument and emotion. Poems and plays use sound, pacing, imagery, figurative language, and line or stage structure to create meaning. A metaphor creates a comparison without requiring literal identity. Worked example: “The streetlights were stars on the road” is a metaphor: streetlights are compared to stars. Ask what brightness, distance, or hope this comparison contributes. lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to develop a qualified argument and rebuttal. An argument is a justified claim, not merely a strong opinion. Strategy: State a claim, give specific evidence, explain its relevance, and address a fair objection.

lessons.objective: Learners will evaluate methods, bias, and source credibility.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to evaluate methods, bias, and source credibility. Research starts with an answerable question, reliable sources, careful notes, synthesis, and attribution. A source’s authorship, date, methods, and possible bias affect what it can establish. Worked example: A city report may document bus ridership; a student interview can add experience but cannot establish citywide ridership alone. Record the title, author or organization, date, and location of information. Strategy: Ask, find, evaluate, take notes in your own words, compare, and cite.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to lead a fair seminar discussion. A clear presentation has an audience, purpose, organization, and relevant evidence. lessons.title: Analyze phonology, orthography, and linguistic variation
lessons.objective: Learners will analyze phonology, orthography, and linguistic variation.
lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to analyze phonology, orthography, and linguistic variation. A spoken word is made of sounds; print represents language with letters and combinations of letters. A phoneme is a contrastive speech sound. A grapheme is a written symbol or symbol group. English spelling is patterned, but spelling and sound are not identical. Worked example: Say “ship” slowly: /sh/ /i/ /p/. The letters s and h jointly represent the first sound. Pronunciation differences among dialects are systematic, not evidence of poor intelligence. Strategy: Listen, segment, connect sounds to print, then test your interpretation in a meaningful sentence.

lessons.passage: During a project at the college linguistics seminar, Noor compared sound changes with surviving spelling conventions. The central observation was that several words kept spellings after pronunciation changed. This finding is important because written conventions can persist longer than spoken habits. The immediate outcome was clear: the seminar separated historical explanation from present-day judgment. The broader claim is more qualified: speech, writing, and social convention interact in complex ways. A critical reader should also consider the limitation: examples alone do not establish a universal rule. The next inquiry should be designed to consult historical dictionaries and phonological corpora. Notice the distinction between an observation, a proposed explanation, a justified conclusion, and what remains unknown. In academic discussion, these distinctions help prevent plausible interpretations from being presented as settled facts. An academic response to this case should make its terms explicit, evaluate the relevance of the available evidence, and explain how the conclusion might change if a competing interpretation were better supported. When studying analyze phonology, orthography, and linguistic variation, avoid turning a descriptive pattern into a universal law without additional evidence. A responsible analysis will present both the claim and its scope, then propose a feasible way to investigate the unresolved question.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to design and critique a research-based literature review. Research starts with an answerable question, reliable sources, careful notes, synthesis, and attribution. A source’s authorship, date, methods, and possible bias affect what it can establish. Worked example: A city report may document bus ridership; a student interview can add experience but cannot establish citywide ridership alone. Record the title, author or organization, date, and location of information. Strategy: Ask, find, evaluate, take notes in your own words, compare, and cite.

lessons.instruction: This lesson focuses on how to critique a presentation for ethics, clarity, and evidence. A clear presentation has an audience, purpose, organization, and relevant evidence. Active listening involves restating meaning accurately, asking thoughtful questions, and responding respectfully. Worked example: Instead of “That is wrong,” try “I heard your claim that the garden needs more water. What measurement supports it?” The second response tests evidence without attacking the person. Strategy: Prepare an opening, supporting points, and a conclusion; listen; confirm understanding.
